Subject: Light Up a Life — draft for Moira’s review, not for publication yet

Our Light Up a Life tree will be in the bookshop window again this year. Hilary asked here the other day whether we were doing it, as her mum’s name was on it last year. Yes, Hilary, we are, and we shall be very pleased to see you and your sister.

It is seven years this month since my husband Ray died at the hospice. The first year I hung his tag on the tree, I could hardly write it. These days I write it at the shop counter, with the same pen. I still take a little time over it, though. You would think writing a name you know so well would be the easiest thing.

I mention that because I know there will be people coming in to write a tag for the first time, as well as those who have been doing it for years. Please don’t feel you have to be cheerful, or explain yourself. If you would like a chat, we are there, but if you would rather quietly write your tag, that is quite all right too.

Memory tags will be available in the shop from Monday 16 November, with a suggested donation of £3. There will be envelopes on the counter if you would rather take yours away and write it at home. Sometimes the words come more easily there.

We will switch on the lights on Saturday 28 November at 4pm. The Gildencroft Primary choir are coming back to sing a few carols, and Doreen is making mince pies again. Those who came last year will know that it is unwise to leave the mince pie part of the evening too late.

All the names on the tags will be read aloud at the hospice remembrance service on Sunday 13 December, at 3pm in the day centre. You do not have to attend the service for the name on your tag to be read.

The tree is for anyone who is grieving, whether or not the person you are remembering was cared for by the hospice. And you are very welcome simply to come and stand beside it. You need not write a tag, buy a book or buy anything at all.

Thank you to everyone who helped make last year’s tree so special. There were 412 tags, and I remember how often someone would stop to look, then stay a little longer than they had meant to. Thank you for bringing your names and memories, for singing with the children, and for making room for one another in a very full little shop.

We shall be glad to see you again, and just as glad to welcome you for the first time.

Jean
